entries.narration: Here is the problem Docker was built to solve. An application is never just its code. To run, it also needs a language runtime, a set of libraries, some operating system packages, and a handful of settings. On your laptop all of those happen to line up. Now copy only the code to a server. The server supplies everything else from whatever it has installed, and months later its runtime is older, its libraries resolved to different versions, and a system library the database driver needs is missing. The same commit fails, and nothing on your laptop reproduces it. That gap is called environment drift. An image closes most of it. The code, the runtime, the libraries and the start command are packaged once, and every machine runs that same artifact, so an update becomes a deliberate rebuild instead of something that happens to you. But be precise about the limit. An image does not contain a kernel. The container uses the host's Linux kernel, and it must match the host's CPU architecture. And the application's data and secrets deliberately stay outside the image. Keep those four in mind: they come back in nearly every chapter.

Containers are often described as lightweight virtual machines. That phrase hides the one difference that matters, so let's put the two side by side. On the left, a hypervisor presents virtual hardware, and each virtual machine boots its own guest kernel and operating system on top of it. The isolation is strong, but every workload pays for a whole operating system in memory and start-up time. On the right, there is no guest kernel at all. Each container is an ordinary process running on the host, and the kernel gives it a restricted view of the system: its own process list, its own filesystem, its own network stack. Every container shares the same host kernel. That is why a container can start in about the time its process takes to start. It also explains three things worth remembering. A Linux container needs a Linux kernel beneath it, which matters on a Mac or Windows laptop. A flaw in that shared kernel can affect every container on the host, so a container boundary is not as strong as a VM boundary. And containers and virtual machines are often used together: plenty of containers run inside cloud virtual machines.

Docker has a small vocabulary, and most confusion comes from mixing up its nouns. There are four objects and four verbs. A Dockerfile is a text file of build instructions. Building it produces an image, which is a read-only template: a set of files plus settings such as the command to start. An image does nothing on its own. When you run it, Docker creates a container, which is an instance of that image with its own writable state, its own logs, and eventually its own exit status. One image can start many containers. On the right of this board, the same image is behind two running API containers and one migration job that has already exited. To get an image from the build machine to the machine that runs it, you push it to a registry and pull it on the other side. In the registry, an image lives in a repository and is found by a tag such as one point zero. A tag is a name that can be moved to different content later; a digest identifies the exact content. Notice also that images and containers belong to one Docker host. A registry is how an image moves between hosts.

When you type a docker command, where does it actually run? Not in your terminal. The docker command is only a client. It turns what you typed into a request to the Docker API, and sends it to a daemon, called dockerd, which does the real work: it pulls images, builds them, and starts and stops containers. The daemon owns those objects. Which daemon receives the request is decided by the current context. The default context usually points at a daemon on this machine, through a local socket. Another context might point at a build server over SSH. Here is why that matters. Each daemon has its own images, its own containers and its own volumes. Run docker ps against the build box and you see its containers, not yours, and nothing in the output says it came from somewhere else. That is harmless for listing. It is not harmless for removing a container or reclaiming disk space, because the operation lands on whichever host the context names. So form one habit early: before anything that changes state, check which context you are in. The registry, at the bottom, is a third party again. The daemon talks to it, not your terminal.

So far we have said a container is an isolated process. Here is what the isolation is made of. The Linux kernel provides two features. Namespaces control what a process can see. In its own PID namespace, the container's main process sees itself as process one, and cannot see the host's other processes. In its own network namespace it has its own interfaces and ports. In its own mount namespace it has a root filesystem assembled from the image. There are a few more, for the hostname, shared memory, and optionally user IDs. The second feature, control groups, or cgroups, limits what a process can use: CPU time, memory, and the number of processes it may start. Docker sets up both for you, but resource limits are only applied if you ask for them, which is a later chapter. Now the platform question. All of this is Linux kernel machinery. On macOS and Windows there is no Linux kernel, so Docker Desktop runs a small Linux virtual machine, and the daemon and every container run inside it. That is why file paths, networking from the host, and file sharing performance on Desktop do not behave exactly like native Linux. When an example depends on that, this course will say so.

Before changing anything, observe. Three read-only commands draw the map we have been building. docker context show prints which daemon your commands are addressed to. docker version reports two things that are easy to conflate: the client version, which is the command-line tool, and the server version, which is the engine that will do the work, along with its operating system and architecture. docker info describes the daemon's world: how many containers and images it holds, where it keeps its data, and what platform it runs on. On Docker Desktop, that platform is the Linux virtual machine, not your laptop. The output on the left is illustrative and trimmed; your versions will differ, and that is the point of recording them. These commands also separate two failures that share one error message. If the daemon is not running, docker version prints its client section and then fails to reach the server. If the context points at the wrong host, you may get an answer from a daemon you did not intend, or no answer at all. Check the context first, then the daemon. And whenever you meet an unfamiliar option, docker, the command name, then dash dash help, is the first reference. Next, we put this map to work by running a container.

Most people meet Docker through one command, docker run, and that hides the fact that it does three separate things. Let's pull them apart, because each one fails differently. docker pull copies an image from a registry into this daemon's local image store. Nothing runs yet; you now simply have a template. docker create makes a container from that image. The container has its configuration and its own writable filesystem, but it is in the created state, with no process at all. docker start launches the container's main process, and the container is now running. When that process ends, for any reason, the container moves to exited. It is not deleted. It keeps its exit code, its logs and its filesystem until you remove it, and you can start it again. docker run folds all of this into one command. It pulls only if the image is missing locally, which means it will not fetch a newer version of a tag you already have. It creates a brand new container every time, so running the same command twice gives you two containers. And it starts the container, attaching your terminal unless you ask for detached mode. Next, we look at those attachment choices.

A container has one main process, and these options decide how your terminal is connected to it. The default is foreground. The process's output streams straight to your terminal, and pressing control C sends it a signal to stop. That suits a one-off task, like checking a configuration file, especially with dash dash rm so the container is removed when it exits. Detached mode, dash d, is the opposite. Docker prints the new container's ID and gives your prompt back, while the process keeps running in the background. A long-running service such as our catalogue API is normally detached, and you read its output later with docker logs. The other two flags are about input. Dash i keeps standard input open, so you can pipe data into the process, for example importing a file of items. Dash t allocates a pseudo-terminal, which programs need for prompts, colours and line editing. They are separate flags, but you will usually see them together, as dash i t, to get an interactive shell inside a container. The rule for choosing is simple: pick the mode the process actually needs. A shell needs a terminal; a web service needs neither, and attaching to it gains you nothing.

Here is one docker run command for the catalogue API, read clause by clause, because each part ends up in a different place. Dash e sets environment variables, here a log level and a data source. They become part of the main process's environment, and the application reads them at start-up. The words after the image name are arguments, and they replace the image's default command for this one container. None of this changes the image. It is runtime configuration, stored with the container. Now the port. Inside its own network namespace, the API listens on port eight thousand and eighty. Nothing outside can reach that port until you publish it. Dash p one two seven dot zero dot zero dot one, colon eight zero eight one, colon eight zero eight zero, opens port eight zero eight one on the host's loopback address and forwards it to the container. So curl on this machine reaches the API, and other machines on the network do not. That is deliberate. If you leave out the address, the port is published on every host interface, which exposes a demo service to your whole network. And if you map to a port the application is not listening on, the connection simply fails. The networking chapter explains why.

Once a container is running, the next skill is looking at it without disturbing it. Three commands, and each reads from a different source. docker logs shows what the main process wrote to standard output and standard error. The daemon captured that stream, so you can read it even after the container has exited. docker inspect returns the daemon's record of the container: its state, the process ID on the host, its configuration, network addresses and mounts. The format option picks out the fields you care about. The third command works differently. docker exec does not read anything from the daemon. It starts a brand new process inside the running container's namespaces. Look at the process list in the card. The catalogue API is still process one; the shell we started is process twenty seven, sitting beside it. That matters, because exec never replaces the main process. If the API exits, the container stops, and the shell goes with it. Exec is for looking around, not for keeping a container alive. One more thing to watch for. docker logs only sees standard output and standard error. An application that writes its logs to a file inside the container hides them from this command.

Stopping a container is a conversation, not a switch. docker stop first sends the signal SIGTERM to the main process, process one. It means: finish what you are doing and exit. A well-behaved service stops taking new requests, completes the ones in flight, and exits. If the process is still running after a grace period, ten seconds by default, Docker sends SIGKILL, which ends it immediately with no chance to clean up. Process one has one surprise. The kernel does not apply default signal behaviour to process one, so if the application has no handler for SIGTERM, the signal is simply ignored. The same happens when a shell script is process one and does not pass the signal on to the real application. Either way, every stop waits out the full grace period and ends in a kill. Running the container with dash dash init puts a tiny init process in front as process one, and it forwards signals properly; the next chapter shows the cleaner fix in the image itself. Afterwards, the exit code tells you what happened. Compare three containers. A batch job that finished its work exits with zero. Our API crashing at start-up exits with one, the application's own failure code. And the API we stopped exits with one hundred and forty three, meaning SIGTERM ended it, or one hundred and thirty seven, meaning SIGKILL did. Same command, three very different stories.

Containers accumulate. Every docker run creates a new one, and exited containers stay until you remove them. Removing one deletes its writable layer and its logs, so the first question is always: which of these are mine? Naming helps. Every container in this chapter is named catalog dash something, so docker ps dash a with a name filter lists exactly the ones we created, running or stopped. Read that list, then remove those names and nothing else. Notice what the list does not show. This daemon also holds a stopped database from another project. docker container prune would remove it along with ours, because prune does not know or care who created what. It removes every stopped container on the daemon. On your own laptop that may be acceptable; on a shared host it is how someone else's data disappears. Removal also explains how you change a container. Its configuration, the ports, the environment and the command, is fixed when it is created. To change it, you stop it, remove it, and run it again with the new options. Anything written inside the old container's filesystem is gone. For short-lived containers, dash dash rm removes them automatically on exit. Keeping data across that replacement is what the storage chapter is about.

Every build starts before the first line of the Dockerfile runs. The dot at the end of docker build dot names the build context: the set of files the builder is allowed to use. The context is gathered and sent to the builder first, and the instructions can only read from it. COPY cannot reach anything outside it. Look at the project folder. It contains what the image needs, the Dockerfile, the source and the dependency list. It also contains things it does not need: the git history, which can be large, and the tests. And it contains one file it must never contain: a dot env file holding the database password. A file called dot dockerignore filters the context, in the same spirit as a gitignore. Each pattern removes matching files before anything is sent. After filtering, the builder receives only the Dockerfile, the source and the dependency list. That is faster, because less is transferred, and safer, because a file that was never sent cannot be copied into the image by a careless instruction later. The habit worth forming is to treat the context as part of the design: it should hold what the image needs to run, and nothing else.

Here is the whole Dockerfile for the catalogue API, and the useful way to read it is to sort its instructions into two kinds. The first kind changes files. FROM starts from the base image's existing layers. WORKDIR creates the application directory. COPY brings in the dependency list and later the source code, and RUN executes a command, here installing libraries, and keeps whatever files it changed. Each of these adds a filesystem layer. Layers are read-only, and identical layers are stored once and shared between images, which is why pulling a second image built on the same base is quick. The second kind changes no files at all. ENV sets default environment variables. EXPOSE records which port the application listens on. USER says which identity the process runs as, and CMD says what to run. These are written into the image's configuration, a small record that docker run reads when it creates a container. EXPOSE deserves a warning, because its name misleads. It documents the port; it does not publish anything. Only dash p at run time makes a port reachable from the host. So an image is exactly two things: a stack of layers, and a configuration record that says how to start it.

The FROM line chooses everything underneath your code: the operating system libraries, the language runtime, the tools, and, easy to forget, the people who maintain them. Most official language images come in variants. The full image includes compilers and build tools and is large. The slim variant drops most of that and suits most applications. The Alpine variant is smaller still, but it uses a different C library, musl instead of glibc, and Python packages that ship precompiled native code for glibc may not install, or may need compiling from source. Size is a poor way to decide. Ask four questions instead. Is it compatible with your dependencies? Is it published for the architecture you will run on, for example both amd64 and arm64? Who publishes it, and do you trust them; an official or verified publisher is a different proposition from an unknown account. And is it maintained, rebuilt promptly when security fixes appear? Then install your dependencies on top deliberately. Pin exact versions in a locked requirements file so a rebuild does not silently pick up new ones. Leave package caches out of the layer. And where system packages are needed, update and install in a single RUN, so the package index is never stale.

Three instructions do most of the work of building the application's filesystem. WORKDIR sets the working directory for every instruction after it, and creates it if needed, so later paths can be relative. COPY brings files in from the build context. RUN executes a command in a temporary container and keeps whatever files it changed as a new layer. The order matters more than it first appears. In this Dockerfile, the dependency list is copied on its own, the libraries are installed, and only then is the source copied. The source is what you edit most, so it goes last. When you change a line of code and rebuild, everything before that final COPY is unchanged and can be reused, and the slow install step does not run again. Chapter seven explains exactly how that reuse works. Now compare two common mistakes. Copying the whole project first, with copy dot dot, means any edit to any file invalidates the install step, and every build reinstalls every library. And writing RUN cd slash app does nothing useful: each RUN starts a fresh shell, so the directory change is lost the moment the instruction ends. WORKDIR is the instruction that persists. The result is a small, predictable tree, owned by root and readable by the process that will run it.

The last few lines of a Dockerfile decide two things about every container made from it: which process becomes process one, and which user it runs as. Start with the process. Written in exec form, as a JSON list, the command runs directly, and the Python application itself is process one. When docker stop sends SIGTERM, the application receives it and shuts down cleanly. Now compare a shell wrapper: a start script run without exec. The shell becomes process one, and the application is its child. SIGTERM goes to the shell, which by default does not pass it on. The application never hears it, and after the grace period the container is killed. That is the ignored-signal branch from the last chapter, and here is its cause. If you need a script, end it with exec, so the application replaces the shell as process one. ENTRYPOINT and CMD work together. ENTRYPOINT is the fixed program. CMD supplies default arguments, which the arguments you pass to docker run replace. Finally, identity. Without a USER instruction the process runs as root. USER ten thousand and one drops that for the running process. The application files remain owned by root and readable, so the running API can use them but cannot modify its own code.

Every setting has to live somewhere, and choosing where decides what you must redo when it changes. Build-time values are baked into the image. ARG is an input to the build itself, such as a version label. ENV sets a default variable that every container starts with, and any container can override it. The code and libraries are build-time too, so changing the code means rebuilding the image. Run-time values belong to one container: environment variables passed with dash e, the published port, the command arguments. Changing those means recreating the container from the same image. No rebuild is needed, and that is the point: one tested image, configured differently in each place it runs. Some values belong in neither. Build arguments and environment defaults are recorded in the image, where anyone with it can read them. And here is the mistake to recognise. A project copied wholesale brings its dot env file into layer four. A later instruction deletes it in layer five. The file is hidden from the final filesystem, but layer four still contains it, and anyone with the image can extract it. Deleting it does not undo the copy. The right tool is a build secret mount, which makes a secret available to one RUN instruction without storing it in any layer. Chapter seven puts it to work.

Images are referred to by name, and the name you usually use, a tag, is less fixed than it looks. A tag such as three point twelve dash slim is a pointer. When the publisher rebuilds the image, for example to include a security fix in the base operating system, they move the tag to the new content. So the same FROM line, built in week one and again in week five, can produce two different images. The tag called latest is nothing special either. It is just a name that someone chose to push to, not a promise of the newest version. A digest is different. It is a hash of the image's exact content, and it cannot be moved. Pinning the base by digest makes the build repeatable: it gives the same result next month as today. But that has a cost. A pinned base never receives fixes on its own, so a pinned image quietly ages. Neither choice is a policy by itself. A controlled update combines them: pin for repeatability, then rebuild on purpose, by moving the pin forward, rebuilding, and testing the result. Give it a new tag, and record the digest of what you tested. That digest is what later chapters will deploy, compare and roll back.

Every container gets a thin writable layer on top of its image's read-only layers. When nothing else is mounted, every file the container writes goes there. If the process changes a file that came from the image, the file is first copied up into the writable layer, so the image itself is never modified and other containers sharing it are unaffected. Now watch what that means for data. We run a PostgreSQL container called scratch db, create a table, and insert three rows. Those rows are files in the container's writable layer. Stopping and starting the same container is harmless: the layer is still there, and so are the rows. But docker rm deletes the container, and the writable layer goes with it. Run the same command again, from the same image, and you get a brand new container with a brand new, empty layer. The query fails because the table does not exist. Nothing went wrong in Docker; this is exactly how it is designed. The writable layer lives precisely as long as its container, which is why replacing containers is cheap. The consequence is simple. Anything you need to keep, such as database files or user uploads, must live somewhere with its own lifetime. That is what mounts are for.

A named volume is the usual home for data a container must keep. The daemon creates and manages it, and its lifetime is separate from any container that uses it. Here we create a volume called catalog pg data and mount it at the directory where the PostgreSQL image keeps its data. Which directory that is depends on the image and its version. We are using postgres sixteen, whose documentation gives slash var slash lib slash postgresql slash data. Other major versions may document a different path, so check the image documentation for yours. Mount at the wrong path and the data still lands in the writable layer. Now replace the container. Stop it, remove it, and run a new one with the same dash v flag. The new container mounts the same volume, and the rows are still there. The container was disposable; the data was not. Where does the volume physically live? Under the daemon's own storage directory, not a path you choose. On Docker Desktop that is inside the Linux virtual machine, not on your Mac or Windows filesystem. And its lifetime is explicit. Removing containers never removes a named volume. Only docker volume rm does, and that deletes the data. So name volumes clearly, list them before deleting, and delete only disposable ones, like catalog scratch here, on purpose.

A bind mount takes a directory on the host and makes it appear at a path inside the container. Nothing is copied: the container reads the same files the host has. That is what makes them so useful during development. Here the project's source folder is mounted over slash app slash src, and the API runs in reload mode. Change a file in your editor, and the running container sees the change at once and reloads, with no rebuild. Because this container only needs to read the code, the mount is read-only. Bind mounts trade portability for that convenience. The host path has to exist, with the right contents, on every machine that runs the command. On Docker Desktop, host files are shared into the Linux virtual machine, which can make large source trees noticeably slower. Two traps are worth knowing. With the short dash v syntax, a host path that does not exist is silently created as an empty directory, which leads to confusing failures; the longer mount syntax reports an error instead. And a writable bind mount lets the container change, or delete, files on your host. So the usual split is simple: bind mounts for source code you are editing, and named volumes for data the application itself owns.

Not everything a container writes deserves to be kept. Caches, scratch files and intermediate results can be rebuilt, and some data should never touch a disk at all. For that there is tmpfs, a filesystem that lives in memory. You mount it at a path, here slash app slash cache, and anything written there stays in the host's memory. It is never written to disk, and it disappears when the container stops, not only when it is removed. That makes it the shortest-lived of the four places a container can write, and the table puts them side by side. The writable layer survives a stop but not removal. Named volumes and bind mounts survive both. tmpfs survives neither. tmpfs has costs. It uses memory, so a cache that grows will compete with the application, and it counts against any memory limit you set. It cannot be shared between containers. And it is a Linux feature: on Docker Desktop the memory belongs to the Linux virtual machine. The decision across this whole chapter comes down to one question about each piece of data: how long must it live? Answer that first, and the choice of storage follows.

Two mount problems regularly masquerade as application bugs, and both have simple mechanical causes. The first is hiding. When you mount something at a path, it replaces whatever the image had there, for as long as the mount exists. Mount an empty host directory over slash app slash src and the application's code vanishes from the container's view, and the API fails at start-up because it cannot find its own module. Named volumes behave slightly differently: when an empty named volume is first mounted, Docker copies the image's files at that path into it. A bind mount is never pre-filled. The second problem is permission. Inside the container the API runs as user ten thousand and one, as we set in the Dockerfile. It tries to save an upload into a bind-mounted directory on the host, and is refused. The evidence is in the numbers. The id command inside the container reports ten thousand and one. ls with the numeric flag on the host shows the directory belongs to one thousand. The kernel compares numeric IDs, never names, so the container simply does not own that directory. Fix it by giving the directory to the container's user ID, or by using a named volume the container can own.

A named volume keeps the catalogue's data safe across container replacement. It does not protect that data from much else. If the disk fails, or someone runs docker volume rm, the volume and everything in it are gone together. So the last part of this chapter is backup, and the one rule worth remembering: a backup is something you have restored. The path has four steps. First, take a logical dump using the database's own tool, which produces a consistent copy even while the database is running. Second, store that dump somewhere other than the volume, ideally off the host entirely. Third, restore it into a disposable database container with its own fresh volume, never over the live one. Fourth, verify: compare row counts, check a few known records, and point the application at the restored database and make a real request. The commands on the left are an outline; the exact options belong to your PostgreSQL version's documentation. Now the false comforts. The volume itself is not a backup. Copying the data directory of a running database may capture files mid-write and produce something that will not start. And a dump nobody has restored is an unknown. Only after a verified restore should any old volume be removed, and then deliberately, by name.

Before configuring anything, let's follow one request from the browser to the database, because every networking problem in this chapter is a break somewhere on this path. Each container runs in its own network namespace. That means it has its own network interfaces, its own set of ports, and its own loopback address. In networking terms, the host, the API container and the database container behave like three separate machines. The request starts in the browser on the host, which connects to port eight zero eight one on the host's loopback address. That port was published, so Docker forwards the connection to the API container's own interface, on port eight thousand and eighty, where the API is listening. To answer, the API opens a second connection: to the name catalog db, on port five four three two, across a private network called catalog net. The database listens there and replies. Two consequences are worth stating now. Because each namespace has its own ports, two containers can both listen on eight thousand and eighty without colliding. And because each has its own loopback, localhost inside one container never reaches another. Exposure is deliberate too: the API is published to this host only, and the database is not published at all.

Containers on one host are connected by bridge networks, a virtual switch the daemon manages. Every Docker host has a default bridge, and any container started without a network option joins it. The default bridge has two drawbacks. Containers on it can reach each other only by IP address, not by name. And unrelated containers, from every project on the host, end up sharing it. The better habit is a user-defined bridge per application. One command, docker network create catalog net, makes one. Start the database and the API with dash dash network catalog net, and three things change. They can find each other by container name. Only members of catalog net are connected to each other, so a container from another project cannot reach the database across this network. And outbound traffic, say to fetch something from the internet, still leaves through the host as before. Membership is flexible. You choose the network at run time, and you can attach a running container later with docker network connect, as we do here with a background worker. A container can belong to several networks at once, which is how you will later let one service talk to two groups without joining those groups to each other. docker network inspect lists exactly who is a member.

How does the API turn the name catalog db into an address? On a user-defined network, Docker runs an embedded DNS server for the members. Inside each container, the resolver is pointed at a special address, one two seven dot zero dot zero dot one one. When the API asks for catalog db, the embedded server answers with that container's current address on the network. Names it does not own, like an external API's hostname, are forwarded on to the host's normal DNS. The terminal shows why this matters. Ask from inside the API, with getent hosts, and catalog db resolves to one seventy two dot eighteen dot zero dot two. Now replace the database container. Its data is safe in the volume, but the new container may get a different address, here dot four. The name still resolves, to the new address, and the API keeps working without any change. If the API had been configured with the old IP, it would now be talking to nothing. You can add extra names with a network alias, for example a short name like db. And remember the scope: names resolve only for members of the same network. A container outside catalog net asking for catalog db gets no answer at all, which is often the first clue to a membership problem.

The word port causes a lot of confusion, because people use it for three different settings that live in three different places. The table lays them out for both services. First, listening. This belongs to the application: the address and port it binds to inside its own namespace. The API listens on eight thousand and eighty, the database on five four three two. If nothing is listening, nothing else in this table matters. Second, EXPOSE. This is a note in the image recording which port the application uses. It opens nothing. Its only practical effect is with dash capital P, which publishes every exposed port on a random host port. Third, publishing. Dash p forwards a port on the host into the container, and it should name the host address too, as we do with one two seven dot zero dot zero dot one, so the API is reachable from this machine only. The database has no published port, so the host cannot reach it at all. Now the misreading worth correcting. Unpublished does not mean private. Every container that is a member of catalog net can connect to the database on five four three two. Publishing controls exposure to the host. Network membership controls who else can connect, and that is the boundary to design.

Here is the single most common networking mistake, and it comes straight from the idea of separate namespaces. The API is configured to reach its database at localhost, port five four three two. On a laptop without containers, that worked. Inside a container, it fails with connection refused. Localhost always means the namespace you are in, and inside catalog api, localhost is catalog api itself. Nothing listens on five four three two there. The fix is to use the other container's name, catalog db, which resolves on the shared network. Sometimes a container genuinely needs a service running on the host itself, perhaps a mock API you started on your laptop. How to reach it depends on the platform, so do not assume one answer. Docker Desktop provides a special name, host dot docker dot internal. On Linux Engine that name does not exist by default; you add it at run time with dash dash add host, mapping it to the special value host gateway. In both cases, the host service must listen on an address the container network can reach, not only on the host's own loopback. Finally, host networking, available on Linux, puts the container in the host's namespace entirely. Its localhost is the host's localhost, but there is no isolation and no port mapping, so use it sparingly.

When a connection fails, resist changing settings at random. Walk the request path and ask four questions in order, each with evidence you can collect. Is the caller a member of the same network as the target? docker network inspect answers that. Does the name resolve, from inside the caller? getent hosts answers that. Is something listening, and on which address and port? And finally, can the caller actually connect? Always test from the caller, not from your laptop, because they sit in different namespaces. The table maps four classic failures to the question that exposes them. A container not on catalog net fails at the name. A wrong port, or localhost used for another container, fails with connection refused. And one failure is subtle enough to show in detail. The application images often lack network tools, so start a throwaway busybox container that shares the API's network namespace, and run netstat. It shows the API listening on one two seven dot zero dot zero dot one, its own loopback only. Publishing forwards connections to the container's interface, where nothing listens, so curl on the host gets a connection reset. The fix belongs in the application's configuration: listen on all interfaces, zero dot zero dot zero dot zero, inside the container, and let publishing decide the exposure.

In the last two chapters we built the catalogue application by hand: a network, a volume, a database container and an API container, each with a long command. Compose lets you write all of that down once, in a file called compose dot yaml, and manage it as a single project. The file declares services. Each service becomes one or more containers, here an API built from our Dockerfile and a database from postgres sixteen. It also declares the volumes and networks those services use. Nothing in it is new: every line corresponds to a choice you already made on the command line. When you run docker compose up, Compose creates real objects and names them after the project, which we have called catalog. The volume becomes catalog underscore pgdata; the containers become catalog api one and catalog db one. It also creates a default network for the project, and on that network each service name resolves, so the API reaches its database simply as db. That is why the file sets the database host to db. The gain is not new capability. It is that the whole setup is reviewable and versioned alongside the code, repeatable on any machine, and labelled, so the project's objects can be found, and removed, as a set.

Compose files contain two kinds of variable, and they are resolved at different moments, in different places. The first is interpolation. A dollar-brace expression like LOG LEVEL, colon dash, info, is filled in by Compose itself, on the host, at the moment it reads the file. It takes the value from a shell variable if one is set, otherwise from a file called dot env beside compose dot yaml, otherwise from the default after the colon dash. That dot env file exists to feed the Compose file. It is not passed into any container. The second kind is the container's environment: the variables the application actually sees when it runs. The environment key sets them directly. The env file key loads a named file of variables into the container. Here the API ends up with LOG LEVEL set to debug, because the dot env file supplied it during interpolation, and the result was written into the container's environment. Mixing the two up is the source of a lot of confusion, so there is one command worth knowing. docker compose config prints the file exactly as Compose sees it, after interpolation. That makes it the quickest way to check a value. It also means the output can contain passwords and tokens, so read it, but do not paste it into a ticket or a chat without looking first.

Every service needs an image, and Compose gets it one of two ways. A build key tells Compose to build the image itself, from a context directory and a Dockerfile, with any build arguments you list. If you also give an image key, Compose uses that as the name of the built image, so the API becomes catalog api, one point four point zero, which is a name you can later push and deploy. A service with only an image key, like the database, is pulled from a registry and never built. That makes the pinning advice from chapter three apply here too, because a tag can move between one pull and the next. One habit to build early: Compose does not rebuild just because the code changed. If the image already exists, up uses it. After changing code, run docker compose up with dash dash build, or docker compose build first. Before running anything, validate. docker compose config dash q checks syntax and the schema, and prints only errors. docker compose config dash dash services lists the services that will actually run, which is useful once overrides enter the picture. Both are read-only. They create nothing, so they are safe to run at any time, including in automated checks before a deployment.

Day to day, a handful of Compose commands cover nearly everything, and they act on the whole project unless you name a service. docker compose up dash d creates whatever is missing and starts it all in the background. docker compose ps shows each service's container, its state and, where a health check exists, its health. docker compose logs with dash f follows the output of one service, here the API. Now change something in the file, say the API's log level, and run up dash d again. Compose compares what is running with what the file now describes, and recreates only the services that differ. The API is replaced; the database is not touched. Shutting down needs more care, so the table spells it out. Stop stops the containers and removes nothing. Down removes the containers and the project's network, but keeps named volumes, so the catalogue's data survives. Down dash v also removes the named volumes. For this project that means catalog underscore pgdata, and with it every row in the database. It is a useful command for a disposable test environment and a destructive one anywhere else. So read the last row of that table again: use dash v only on purpose, and only when a verified backup exists, as the storage chapter described.

Start-up order is one of the most misunderstood parts of Compose, because the phrase the database is up hides three different states. The process can have started while the database is still initialising and refusing connections. A health check, here pg is ready, can pass, meaning the server accepts connections. And the API's real queries can succeed, which is the only thing a user cares about. Depends on, written as a plain list, makes Compose start the database before the API, but waits only for the process to start. Adding condition service healthy makes Compose wait until the health check passes before starting the API. On shutdown the order reverses: down stops the API first, then the database. That solves start-up. It does not solve what happens afterwards. Depends on is checked once, when the project comes up. If the database restarts an hour later, for an upgrade or a crash, Compose does not pause the API or restart it in step. The API's connections fail, and the only real fix lives in the application: it must retry, reconnecting with a backoff instead of giving up. And note that health status on its own restarts nothing. It reports. What acts on failure, restart policies, comes in the diagnosis chapter.

The same application runs differently on a laptop and on a server, and copying the whole Compose file for each environment guarantees the copies drift apart. The better pattern is one base file plus small override files. The base, compose dot yaml, holds what every environment shares: the services, the health checks and dependencies, the volume. For development, a file called compose dot override dot yaml is special: when it exists beside the base file, Compose merges it in automatically. That is where development conveniences go: the bind-mounted source from the storage chapter, the reload command, debug logging. For production, you name the files explicitly with dash f, the base and then compose dot prod dot yaml. When you name files yourself, the automatic override is not read, so none of the development conveniences leak into production. The production file adds what production needs: an image pinned to a tested version instead of a build, no source mount, and a restart policy. Merging has rules. Later files override or extend earlier ones, but different settings merge differently: some values are replaced, others are combined. Rather than predicting the result, ask for it. docker compose config, with the same dash f flags, prints exactly what will run.

The database password has been sitting in plain sight in our examples, so this section puts it where it belongs. A secret should reach the running process at run time, never through the image and never written into the Compose file. Compose's secrets feature does that with a file. The password lives in a file on the host, and that file is listed in dot gitignore, so it never reaches the repository. The secrets section names it, and each service that lists the secret sees it at slash run slash secrets slash db password, mounted read-only. The official Postgres image already understands this: give it POSTGRES PASSWORD FILE, and it reads the password from that path. Our API accepts the same convention. Why a file rather than an environment variable? Environment variables appear in docker inspect, are easy to log by accident, and are inherited by every child process. A file has to be deliberately opened. Now the limits, because this is easy to overestimate. On the host, the secret is a plain text file. Anyone who can run docker commands can read it through exec. Changing it means editing the file and recreating the containers, and nothing records who read it. This is a delivery mechanism, not a secret-management system, and production may need a real one.

Every image you have built so far went through BuildKit, the build engine behind docker build. The command you type is a client, and the work happens in a builder. Buildx is the part of the CLI that lets you choose which builder, and where the result goes. The default builder runs inside the Docker daemon, which is why your images have simply appeared in docker images. You can create others with docker buildx create. A builder using the docker container driver runs BuildKit in its own container, and supports features the default one may not, such as exporting caches or building for several platforms at once. docker buildx ls lists your builders and the platforms each can build for. Each builder keeps its own cache, so switching builders means starting cold. The result needs a destination. Dash dash load copies it into the local image store, where docker run can use it. Dash dash push sends it to a registry. Dash dash output can write the final filesystem as files or a tarball, useful for build artefacts that are not images. And here is the trap. Build with a container builder and give no output, and the build succeeds, but the image exists only in that builder's cache. docker images will not show it, and docker run will not find it.

Chapter three promised to explain why the order of a Dockerfile matters. The build log is the evidence. Here is the same Dockerfile rebuilt after two different edits. On the left, we changed one line of application source. Every step up to the last is marked cached, and only the final COPY ran, in a fraction of a second. On the right, we changed the dependency list. The COPY of that file now has different content, so it runs, and because one step missed, every step after it reruns too, including a forty second install. That is the rule. A step is reused when the instruction and its inputs are unchanged. For COPY, the input is the actual content of the files being copied, not their timestamps. And a single miss invalidates the rest of the build. So put the things that change rarely first, and the things that change often last. The cache can also be wrong in a quieter way. A RUN that updates package indexes looks identical every time, so it is reused, and new security updates never arrive. Freshness must be deliberate. Dash dash pull checks the registry for a newer base image. Dash dash no cache reruns every step. Use them on a schedule, not by accident.

Some Python libraries, including the PostgreSQL driver when built from source, need a C compiler and development headers to install. The application never needs them to run. In a single-stage build, those tools end up in the image you ship. A multi-stage build separates the two jobs. Each FROM line with an AS name starts a new stage. The build stage starts from the slim base, installs the compiler and headers, creates a virtual environment, and installs the dependencies into it. The runtime stage starts again from a clean base, adds only the small runtime library the driver needs, and then copies just one thing from the build stage: the finished virtual environment. COPY dash dash from equals build is the bridge. Everything else in the build stage, the compiler, the headers, the download cache, is simply left behind. What do you gain? The shipped image no longer contains a compiler, which means fewer packages to patch and fewer tools for an attacker to use. It is usually smaller too, but by how much depends entirely on the application, so measure it with docker image ls and docker history rather than trusting a number from a blog. Two working tips: dash dash target build stops at the build stage so you can debug it, and independent stages can build in parallel.

The layer cache is all or nothing: a step is either reused completely or run again from scratch. When the dependency list changes, the install step reruns and downloads every package again, even the ninety percent that did not change. A cache mount fixes that. Adding mount type equals cache to a RUN gives the step a directory, here pip's own download cache, that persists in the builder across builds. When the step reruns, pip finds most packages already downloaded. The cache directory is never part of the image, so it costs nothing at run time. Continuous integration adds a different problem. Many CI systems give each job a fresh machine, which means a fresh, empty builder and no layer cache at all. Every build starts cold. Exported caches solve it. Dash dash cache to writes the build cache somewhere durable, such as a registry reference or the CI system's own cache service, and dash dash cache from lets the next job import it and start warm. Mode equals max includes the intermediate build stages too. Two rules keep this honest. Caches only save time: a completely cold build must still produce a correct image. And only import caches from a location you control, because a cache is build input, and anyone who can write to it can influence what you ship.

Chapter three showed the wrong way to give a build a credential: copy it in, delete it later, and leave it sitting in an earlier layer. Here is the right way, and its limits. The catalogue's dependencies include a package from a private index, which needs a token. You pass the token to the build with dash dash secret, naming an id and a source file. In the Dockerfile, only a RUN instruction that declares mount type equals secret with that id can see it. It appears as a file under slash run slash secrets for the duration of that one step, and then it is gone. No layer contains it, and the image history does not record it. Private git repositories work the same way through the SSH mount. Dash dash ssh default forwards your SSH agent into the build, so git clone can authenticate, but the private key itself is never copied into the build at all. Now the limits, which matter as much as the feature. The mount protects the layer. It cannot protect against the command you run. A step that echoes the token, a shell with tracing switched on, or a tool in verbose mode can print it into the build log. A step that writes it into a file or a configuration file puts it straight back into a layer. And passing it as ARG or ENV records it in the image.

Containers share the host's kernel, and they also share its CPU. An image built for one architecture will not run on another. That used to be rare. Now it is common: a developer on an ARM laptop, deploying to x86 servers. Build there without thinking, push, and the image is arm64 only. On the amd64 server, the container fails at once with exec format error, a message that does not mention architecture at all. The fix is to build for both, and publish them under one tag. docker buildx build with dash dash platform linux amd64 comma linux arm64 builds two images, and pushes an image index: a small list that maps each platform to its own image digest. Inspect it, and you see both entries. When a host pulls the tag, it reads the index and takes the variant that matches. That also means the digest of the tag and the digest of the image a server actually runs are different things, which matters in the delivery chapter. Producing the second platform has three strategies with different costs. Emulation runs the other architecture in software: simple, but much slower. Native nodes give the builder a real machine per architecture. Cross-compilation builds on one machine for another, which is fast where the toolchain supports it. For Python, check that native wheels, and the base image, exist for both.

Isolation is the starting point, not the result. A container is only as contained as the authority you hand back to it, so this chapter begins with a review. Start with the daemon. It runs as root, and it can start any container with any options, including one that mounts the host's entire filesystem. That means anyone who can talk to the daemon's socket is, in practice, root on the host. Membership of the docker group grants exactly that, and so does a remote API without proper authentication. Now the configuration on the left, which is the kind of thing that gets copied from a forum post. The API runs privileged, which gives it every capability and access to host devices. It mounts the Docker socket, which hands it control of the daemon. It bind-mounts the host's root filesystem, read and write. And it runs as root. Ask of each line: what does the catalogue API actually need? It needs none of them. It needs to listen on a port, read its own files, connect to the database, and write uploaded images somewhere. So the review removes each grant. One of these needs an application change, not just a configuration change: the API must write only to one directory it owns, which then becomes its only writable mount.

Two security controls sound alike and are often confused, so it helps to place them precisely. A non-root user, set with USER in the image as we did in chapter three, controls the process inside the container. The catalogue API runs as user ten thousand and one instead of root. If an attacker takes over that process, they have that user's limited rights inside the container. But the daemon that started it still runs as root on the host. Rootless mode changes the daemon itself. The daemon, and every container it starts, runs as an ordinary unprivileged user on the host, using user namespaces. Root inside a container is mapped to an unprivileged range of user IDs outside it. That has costs: binding ports below one thousand and twenty four needs extra configuration, and some network and storage features behave differently, so check the documentation for your platform. The table shows why neither control is enough alone. With a rootful daemon and a root process, a container escape lands as host root. A non-root user improves that. Rootless mode improves it differently, and the two together leave an escape with almost nothing. And still, neither removes the need to grant only the authority a service needs.

On Linux, root is not one power but a collection of them, called capabilities: changing file ownership, binding low-numbered ports, configuring the network, mounting filesystems, and many more. A container does not receive all of them. Docker grants a reduced default set, enough for typical software to work, and leaves out the most powerful ones, such as the broad administrative capability called SYS ADMIN. The privileged flag throws that reduction away. It grants every capability, gives the container access to the host's devices, and relaxes the security profiles that normally confine the process. A privileged container is close to running directly on the host as root. It is occasionally necessary for tools that manage the host itself, and almost never for an application. Least authority goes the other way: start from nothing and add back only what a named requirement needs. Our API listens on port eight thousand and eighty, above the low-port range, and does nothing else that needs a capability, so it drops them all. If a service genuinely must bind port eighty, it adds back exactly that one, and the reason is written down beside it. Finally, no new privileges stops a process from gaining rights through setuid programs, closing a common escalation path.

The previous sections limited what a container may do with the kernel. This one limits two things an attacker would do next: change files, and reach other systems. First, the filesystem. Setting read only to true mounts the container's root filesystem read-only, so a compromised process cannot modify the application's code or drop tools into system directories. Applications still need somewhere to write, so we give exactly two places: slash tmp as a memory-backed tmpfs, and slash app slash uploads as one named volume. This is the application change from the first section paying off: because the API was told where its writable directory is, the rest can be locked. Second, the network. Instead of one network for everything, there are two. Frontend carries the API, which is published to this host only. Backend carries the API and the database. The database is on backend alone, so nothing else can reach it, and backend is marked internal, which means it has no route to the outside world. A compromised database cannot fetch tools or send stolen data out over that network. None of these restrictions is a wall on its own. Each one narrows what an attacker can do after a first foothold, and together they turn one mistake into a contained incident.

Vulnerability scanners compare the packages in an image against databases of known issues, and they produce long lists. That list is evidence. It is not a decision, and treating every line the same way either buries a team in work or trains it to ignore the report. The findings here are illustrative, with placeholder identifiers, and each one ends differently. A flaw in the base image's TLS library, with a fix available, on a path the API really uses: rebuild on the patched base. A flaw in the web framework, fixed only in a new major version: upgrade it, run the tests, and release, because compatibility is part of the fix. A flaw in an image library with no fix yet, in code the catalogue never calls: accept it, but record who decided, why, and when that decision expires. And a flaw in a tool that is not even present at run time: the multi-stage build already removed it. So read each finding for reachability, for whether a compatible fix exists, and for exposure. Severity alone does not set the order. Finally, compare two images a month later. The pinned digest never changes, so its findings only grow as new issues are published. The rebuilt, tested image has a new digest, and that is the one to record and deploy.

Two kinds of evidence travel with a well-built image. A software bill of materials, or SBOM, is an inventory: every package and version inside the image. Its value appears on the day a new vulnerability is announced. Instead of guessing, you search your SBOMs and know within minutes which images contain the affected version. An SBOM says what is inside; it does not say that any of it is safe. Provenance records how the image was built: which source repository and commit, which builder, which parameters. It lets you trace a running image back to the code that produced it. Both are claims, and a claim is only as good as its producer. Evidence attached by an unknown party proves nothing, so the producer's identity has to be verified; the exact tools for doing that belong to their own documentation. Now the bad day. A credential has been exposed, perhaps pushed in an image layer, perhaps printed in a build log. The order matters. Revoke it at the issuer first, so it stops working. Then rotate: issue a new one and deliver it the right way. Find every place the old one was used, including images that baked it in, rebuild and redeploy them, and check the logs for misuse. Deleting the image is not on this list, because copies already exist in caches, registries and pulls.

Delivery starts with knowing exactly what an image reference says. Read it left to right. First the registry host, here registry dot example, with an optional port: the server where the image lives. Then a namespace, usually a team or organisation, and a repository, one line of images such as the catalogue API. Then either a tag, after a colon, or a digest, after an at sign. From earlier chapters you know the difference: a tag is a movable name, and a digest identifies exact content. Short forms hide several of these parts. postgres colon sixteen really means docker dot io, slash library, slash postgres, colon sixteen: the default registry and the namespace for official images. Leave off the tag entirely and you get latest, which is only a name somebody chose to push to. For anything you deploy, write the full address, so nobody has to guess which registry was meant. Pushing and pulling private images needs authentication. docker login stores a credential for one registry. Where it is stored matters: a credential helper keeps it in the operating system's keychain rather than in a plain text file in your home directory. In automation, use a short-lived token from the CI system's secret store, with only the rights the job needs.

When you push an image, the registry reports a digest: a hash that names exactly what was uploaded. Pull by that digest, with an at sign, and you get exactly that content, every time, from any machine. Pull by a tag twice, a week apart, and you may get two different images, because the tag can be moved. For a multi-platform release there is one more layer, introduced in chapter seven. The tag one point four point zero points at an image index, and the index has its own digest. Inspect it, and the index lists one image per platform, each with a different digest of its own. When an amd64 server pulls the release, it reads the index and runs the amd64 image, whose digest is not the index digest. So which do you write down? Both have a job. Deploy by the index digest. It is one stable reference that works on every platform the release supports, and it can never be repointed. Then record the platform digest of what actually ran on each host. When you later compare a running container with a vulnerability report, or prove what was in production last Tuesday, that platform digest is the precise answer.

A delivery pipeline turns a commit into a published image, and its most important property is what it refuses to publish. Here is an illustrative one, written as a plain shell script rather than for any particular CI product. It stops at the first failure. It builds the image and tags it with the commit hash, so every image can be traced to its source. It then starts the image, binding the test port to the loopback address, and waits for the health endpoint to answer. Starting is not enough, so it makes a representative request, listing items, and checks that the response actually contains data. Only if both checks pass does it push the image, and the last step records the digest that was published, as evidence for later. The order is the safety. If the container fails to start, or answers with an error, the job stops before the push, and the registry never sees the broken image. Everything in the registry has, at minimum, started and answered a real request. Two honest notes. Clean up the test container whether the checks pass or fail. And remember these checks prove a floor, not perfection: they catch an image that cannot start or serve, not every bug the release might contain.

A tested image is valuable precisely because it was tested, so the aim is to run that same image everywhere. Build once, then let each environment configure it. Look at what stays the same: the image, identified by its digest, and therefore every line of code and every library that passed the checks in the pipeline. Look at what changes. Staging and production use different databases, different log levels, and different ways of being published. All of that is runtime configuration, supplied as environment variables and settings, exactly as chapter three separated build time from run time. Each environment also has its own secrets, supplied at run time as secret files, never shared between environments and never inside the image. The anti-pattern is tempting: rebuild the image for each environment, baking in the production database address. But every rebuild produces a new artifact that nobody tested. The base image may have moved, a dependency may have resolved differently, and if a secret was baked in, it now leaks into every copy of that image, in every registry and cache. So here is a simple check worth automating. The digest running in staging and the digest running in production should be identical. If they differ, production is running something staging never ran.

Once an image has passed staging, promoting it to production should move a decision, not new bytes. The common shortcut is a tag called prod, moved to each release. The table shows why that is fragile. On Monday, prod points at the tested digest. On Wednesday, someone pushes a different image with the same tag, perhaps by mistake, and the same deployment file now runs code nobody tested. Nothing in the file changed, so nothing in review caught it. The fix is to deploy by digest. The production Compose file names the image by the digest recorded in the pipeline. Promotion is then a one-line change to that file, made in review like any other change. To replace the running service, pull the pinned digest and run up dash d for that service only; Compose recreates just the API, and the database is untouched. Then write down what happened. Which digest was deployed, and which one it replaced. Which checks ran afterwards, such as the health endpoint and a representative request, and whether they passed. Who released it, when, and from which commit. That record turns the next incident into a lookup instead of an investigation, and the previous digest in it is exactly what you will need if you have to roll back.

Rollback sounds simple: redeploy the previous digest. For many releases it is. Version one point four point one changed only the sort order of the catalogue. The database schema did not change, so redeploying the one point four point zero digest puts everything back exactly as it was. Now version one point five point zero. Its migration renames the price column. Deploy it, discover a bug, and redeploy the old image, and the old image fails immediately, because it queries a column that no longer exists. The image rolled back; the data did not. Undoing the data means restoring the backup taken before the migration, and every order written since then is lost. That is why rollback has to be planned before the release, not invented during the incident. Four prerequisites. The previous digest is recorded, and still available in the registry. A verified backup exists from just before the migration, as the storage chapter described. Schema changes are made in an expand then contract style: add the new column now, keep the old one working, and remove it only in a later release, once nothing uses it. And someone has actually tested the old image against the new schema, so you know rollback works before you need it.

Chapter one mentioned that cgroups can limit what a container uses. Now we set those limits, because without them one misbehaving container can starve every other service on the host. The important thing to understand is that each limit fails in its own way. A memory limit is enforced by killing. When the processes in the container try to use more memory than the limit allows, the kernel's out-of-memory killer ends one of them. If that is the main process, the container exits with code one three seven, and docker inspect reports OOM killed as true. A CPU limit is enforced by slowing. Cpus one point zero allows one core's worth of processor time. Ask for more and the process is throttled: it keeps running, but more slowly, which shows up as latency rather than as a crash. A process limit is enforced by refusing. Pids limit caps the number of processes and threads, and an application that tries to start one more gets an error. Setting limits well starts with measurement. Find normal and peak usage, then leave headroom above the peak. And make the application fit inside them: a connection pool, a cache or a worker count sized for a large machine will hit a small limit quickly.

docker stats shows live resource use for each running container. The useful skill is reading it against the limits from the previous section. CPU percent counts cores, so one hundred percent means one full core and two hundred and fifty means two and a half. Memory usage is shown against a limit. If you set none, the limit column shows the total memory available, which can make an unlimited container look harmless right up until it is not. PIDS counts processes and threads. Dash dash no stream prints a single snapshot, which is what you want when recording evidence. Now read the sample. The API is using ninety percent of its two hundred and fifty six megabyte limit; one busy moment and the out-of-memory killer will end it. Its CPU is at almost exactly one core, which is its cap, so it is being throttled and requests will be slow. The database is comfortable. Finally, remember whose capacity this is. Every container shares one host. On Docker Desktop, the host is the Linux virtual machine, with its own fixed share of memory and CPUs, so the numbers are relative to that, not to your laptop. And limits are promises, not reservations: they can add up to more than the machine actually has.

A full disk is one of the most disruptive failures there is, because everything that writes stops at once: the database, the logs, even the builds you would use to fix it. So when space runs low, measure before you delete. docker system df totals the space used by images, containers, local volumes and the build cache, and shows how much of each it considers reclaimable. Add dash v and it lists every object, so you can see whose each one is. Then sort what you find into three kinds. Rebuildable things can be recreated: images can be pulled or built again, and build cache only costs time. Stopped containers you own can usually go. Data is different. Volumes hold records, and deleting one deletes them. And there is evidence: the stopped container that failed last night still holds its logs and its exit state, so keep it until someone has read them. Logs deserve their own attention, because they grow quietly. Everything an application writes to standard output is stored by Docker's logging driver, on the host's disk. Without rotation configured, a chatty service can fill a disk on its own. How rotation is configured depends on the logging driver in use, so check that driver's documentation rather than copying settings blindly.

When something goes wrong, the temptation is to start changing settings. A better habit is to let the first piece of evidence tell you which layer to look at. The table shows four classic failures. A container that exits at start-up with a traceback in its logs has an application problem, in its code or configuration. A container killed under load, with exit code one three seven and OOM killed set to true, hit its memory limit. Writes failing with no space left on device point to storage. And every request failing with connection refused to the database points to the network, or to the database itself. One of these needs care. Exit code one three seven only means the process received SIGKILL, and many things send SIGKILL, including docker stop when the grace period runs out. So check the OOM killed field before blaming memory. The terminal shows two containers with the same exit code and different causes. Not every problem is a crash. If the API is slow, look at CPU. At its cap, with everything slow, it is being throttled. Low, with only the pages that query the database slow, the database is the bottleneck. Either way, form a hypothesis and test it with one change, not five.

Two mechanisms are often confused here: restart policies and health checks. A restart policy decides what happens when the container's main process exits. The default is no, so nothing restarts. On failure restarts after a non-zero exit, optionally up to a maximum count. Always restarts after any exit and when the daemon itself starts. Unless stopped behaves the same, except that it respects a container you stopped deliberately. Restart policies are good at recovering from a crash that will not happen again. They are bad at hiding a crash that happens every time. The terminal shows the result: a container whose status reads restarting, with a restart count of seventeen and climbing. Docker waits a little longer between each attempt, but the cause, perhaps a missing setting, is still there. Read the logs before anything else. The other line is more surprising. The database is up, but unhealthy: its health check has been failing for a while. Plain Docker reports that status and does nothing about it. It does not restart an unhealthy container. Health checks feed decisions: depends on conditions in Compose, your monitoring, or an orchestrator that is designed to replace unhealthy instances. Without one of those, acting on health is your job.

Recovery decisions are made under pressure, and the two costly mistakes are deleting the wrong thing and assuming a backup works. Evidence protects against both. If the problem is space, take an inventory first, with docker system df dash v, so you know what is using the disk and whose it is. Reclaim in order of how cheaply each thing comes back: the build cache first, which costs only rebuild time, then your own old images, by name rather than with a broad prune. Keep failed containers until someone has read their logs, because they are the evidence. And never free space by deleting a volume that has no verified backup. If the problem is data, prove the recovery before relying on it. Restore the latest dump into an isolated stack, with its own volume and its own network, so nothing can touch production by accident. Then check two different things. Records: row counts and a few known samples. And behaviour: point the API at the restored database and make real requests, because data that loads but breaks the application is not a recovery. Write down how long it took, and how much data was written after the dump and is therefore missing. With that evidence, the decision between restarting, rolling back and restoring becomes a choice, not a guess.

This last chapter steps back and looks at the catalogue application as a whole, the way you would before calling it production-ready. Every chapter added one decision, and the board gathers them, grouped by what each one protects. Exposure: there is one public entry point, a reverse proxy; the API is published only on the loopback address behind it; and the database is not published at all, sitting on an internal network. Runtime: the API runs from an image pinned by digest, the same one staging tested. It runs as a non-root user, with every capability dropped and a read-only root filesystem. It has memory, CPU and process limits, a health check and a restart policy, and its logs go to standard output with rotation configured. Its secrets arrive as files, never in the image or the environment. Data: the database lives in a named volume, a dump is taken every night and stored off the host, and a restore is rehearsed and timed every month. The bottom row matters most, because Docker cannot provide it. The application itself must handle SIGTERM and finish its in-flight requests, retry its database connection with a backoff, and write only to the paths it was given. Containers make good behaviour possible; they do not supply it.

Reproducibility is a simple idea with a demanding requirement: you cannot reproduce what you did not write down. The table is the version record this course has asked for since chapter one, applied to the running system. It lists the Docker Engine, Docker Desktop where it is used, the Compose plugin and Buildx. It includes the Dockerfile frontend, which the syntax line at the top of a Dockerfile selects, because it decides which build features are available. It names the API image and the database image by digest, and the application's dependency lock by its hash. Each value comes from the system itself, not from memory: docker version, docker compose version, docker buildx version, and the release record kept by the pipeline. The record has three jobs. It lets you rebuild the same thing months later. It lets you compare two environments when one behaves differently, which is usually the fastest route to a cause. And it tells you which version of the documentation to read, because behaviour and options change between releases. One honest note. The values here are placeholders, because this course asserts no specific versions; its output has been illustrative throughout. Your record should contain real values, captured from your own systems.

A runbook is the procedure written down before it is needed, so that a release, or a recovery, does not depend on memory or on who is on call. Here is a release runbook for the catalogue, followed through once. Before anything changes, three prerequisites are checked: staging ran this exact digest and passed; a backup was restored successfully this week; and the previous digest is written down. If any of these fails, the release waits. The release itself is short. Pin the new digest in the production Compose file, pull it, and run up dash d for the API only, leaving the database untouched. Then check the health endpoint and make a real request. Now the decision point, which is the reason runbooks exist. If the checks pass, record the release and keep watching for an hour. If they fail, do not improvise: roll back to the previous digest first, restore service, and investigate afterwards. Because the release did not change the schema, that rollback is safe, which was itself checked beforehand. Maintenance belongs on a calendar too. Every week, rebuild on the patched base image with pull, and review the new scanner findings. Every month, run a timed restore drill. Problems found by a schedule are much cheaper than problems found by an outage.

Everything in this course has run on one host, and a single host is a single point of failure. So walk through the worst case: the machine is gone, disk and all. What survives is whatever was stored somewhere else. The images are in the registry, identified by digest. The Compose files and configuration are in version control. The secrets are in a secret store. And last night's database dump is stored off the host. From those four, a new host can be built and the application brought back. What is lost is whatever lived only on that host. The database volume is gone, and with it every write made since the dump; that gap is the price of the backup schedule, so it should be a known, accepted number. Logs that were never shipped elsewhere are gone. The build cache is gone too, which only costs time. And any change somebody made by hand on the server, and never committed, is gone for good. Finally, be precise about what recovered means. The processes running is one thing. The data restored, with the gap known, is another. And users being served, proven by a real request, is the only one that counts. Report all three separately, because a running container in front of an empty database is not a recovery.

Compose on a single host covers a great deal: building, configuring, securing, releasing and recovering a real application. It also has a boundary, and knowing where it lies is part of operating well. The table compares responsibilities. On one host, a restart policy restarts a crashed container, but replacing a running, unhealthy one is your job. Losing the host means rebuilding, as the previous section showed. Spreading load over several machines, and rolling releases without downtime, are limited or manual. A cluster scheduler, such as Kubernetes or Swarm, takes these on: it replaces unhealthy containers, reschedules them onto another machine when a host fails, and runs replicas behind a rolling release. Look at the last row, though. Database backup and restore remain your responsibility, with or without a cluster. Replication keeps copies in step, which means a bad write or a dropped table is copied faithfully to every replica. Replicas are not backups. And everything in this course still applies inside a cluster: images by digest, least authority, secrets at run time, evidence before action. Where next? Linux operations for the host underneath, CI and CD for pipelines in depth, cloud container services, or a Kubernetes or Swarm course. Whichever you choose, check the current documentation, and keep the recovery evidence.
